(CNN) -- A college student who survived a boat sinking along with four others said Monday that a safety officer who perished aboard their vessel was a hero for remaining behind and pushing him to safety. Steven Guy, a sailor from Texas A&M University, said that Roger Stone saved both him and another sailor by guiding them out of danger.

"He is my hero," Guy said. "He saved me. If it wasn't for him, I would not be here."

The mariners recounted that they never saw Stone again after he pushed the two men out through a hatch in the boat. Stone, the vessel's second safety officer, was found dead by the Coast Guard on Sunday afternoon.

The two men described spending an entire day adrift in open water after their vessel sank in the Gulf of Mexico. The survivors -- four university students and a safety officer -- told the Coast Guard they had been forced off their sailboat after it took on water and capsized early Saturday. The five survivors were located and airlifted to land at approximately 2 a.m. Sunday, the Coast Guard reported.

The group had to abandon the rapidly sinking sailboat so quickly that they managed to secure only four safety vests for five people, safety officer Steve Conway said Monday. They were compelled to huddle together in the water to keep one another afloat, he explained.

"With five people and four life jackets, we had to watch the person without the life jacket closely," he said. "These young men did a tremendous job. They pulled themselves through. They had a fierce will to live."

R. Bowen Loftin, CEO and vice president of Texas A&M at Galveston, extended his condolences to the Stone family in a letter posted alongside status updates on the school's website.

"We hope they can take some comfort in knowing all five survivors of this tragic accident credit Mr. Stone with heroic efforts that were instrumental in making possible their survival," Loftin wrote. "We now know that Roger Stone died a hero in the classic sense of the word."

Conway recounted that as the group huddled in the water, they watched rescue jets pass overhead three times before finally being spotted.

"It is really discouraging when a plane comes out and flies over and leaves," he said.

Coast Guard Lt. Justo Rivera, who piloted the aircraft that rescued the men, told CNN affiliate KHOU that a flashlight had proven crucial to their survival. While conducting search patterns, Coast Guard members detected the light through their night vision goggles, Rivera said. It was being held aloft by one of the men. Because the Coast Guard was scouring such a vast expanse, the flashlight was "instrumental" to the rescue, he noted.

"It's your proverbial needle in a haystack," Rivera told KHOU.

Throughout the 26-hour ordeal, the group was nibbled at by curious reed fish and circled by a creature whose triangular fin protruded from the water like that of a shark.

"They bumped up against us and kind of nibbled on our clothes," Conway said. "You don't know how big the thing is and how hungry it is. I was always aware of the risk of sharks."

The group's sailboat, named the Cynthia Woods, was one of roughly two dozen vessels traveling from Galveston, Texas, to Veracruz, Mexico, for the annual Veracruz Regatta race, which had begun on Friday.

# Coast Guard Rescues College Sailors After Capsizing in Gulf of Mexico; Safety Officer Dies Saving Crew

**Tragedy strikes competitive sailing team during weekend regatta as beloved safety coordinator sacrifices his life**

---

*(CNN)* — A routine collegiate sailing competition turned to tragedy this weekend when a training vessel capsized in the choppy waters of the Gulf of Mexico, leaving five college students stranded but alive — thanks in large part to a safety officer who lost his life ensuring their survival.

The incident occurred Saturday afternoon approximately 12 miles off the coast, when sudden weather conditions overwhelmed the 34-foot sailing vessel carrying members of a university sailing team during a regional regatta.

## A Sudden Turn

According to preliminary reports from the U.S. Coast Guard, the vessel encountered rapidly deteriorating conditions when a squall line moved through the area, producing wind gusts that witnesses estimated exceeded 40 knots.

"The weather changed in a matter of minutes," said one team member who spoke on condition of anonymity while grieving. "One moment we were racing, and the next we were fighting to stay afloat."

The boat capsized around 2:15 p.m., throwing all six people aboard into the water. While all crew members were wearing personal flotation devices, the rough seas and distance from shore created a life-threatening situation.

## An Act of Sacrifice

Team safety officer **Michael Reyes**, 34, a veteran sailor who had volunteered with the collegiate program for six years, immediately began organizing the students and ensuring each was secured to available flotation.

Survivors credit Reyes with keeping the group calm and together during the more than two hours they awaited rescue.

"He kept telling us to stay connected, to keep our heads above water, to not panic," recalled one student. "He gave his own emergency locator to another team member whose device had malfunctioned."

Witnesses reported that Reyes repeatedly dove beneath the overturned hull to retrieve safety equipment and helped position injured students. During one of these efforts, he was struck by debris and swept away from the group.

Coast Guard rescue swimmers recovered Reyes approximately 40 minutes after their arrival, but he was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital.

## The Rescue

A commercial fishing vessel first responded to the emergency beacon, alerting the Coast Guard, which dispatched a rescue helicopter and cutter to the scene.

"These young sailors did everything right," said a Coast Guard spokesperson. "They stayed together, they had functioning safety equipment, and they had strong leadership in the water. That combination saved lives."

All five students were transported to area hospitals, treated for hypothermia and minor injuries, and are expected to make full recoveries.

## A Community in Mourning

The university released a statement Sunday describing Reyes as "the heart of our sailing program" and confirming that grief counselors would be made available to students, faculty, and staff.

"Michael dedicated himself to keeping our young sailors safe," the statement read. "In his final moments, he embodied everything we strive to teach: courage, selflessness, and an unwavering commitment to those in his care."

Reyes, a former competitive sailor himself, is survived by his wife and two young children. A memorial fund has been established to support his family.

## Investigation Underway

The Coast Guard and university officials have launched a joint investigation into the incident, examining weather forecasting, safety protocols, and equipment readiness.

Sailing safety experts note that while collegiate sailing maintains a strong safety record, incidents like this underscore the importance of rigorous preparation and experienced supervision.

"The ocean demands respect," said a maritime safety consultant unaffiliated with the university. "This is a heartbreaking reminder that even well-trained teams can face conditions beyond anyone's control — and of how much a single dedicated individual can matter."

Funeral arrangements for Reyes are pending. The university has announced it will honor his memory at the season's remaining events.

---

# Twelve Hours in the Water: How Four Fishermen Survived the Capsizing of the *Marlene J*

*A harrowing tale of survival off the coast when a routine fishing trip turned into a fight for life*

---

The forecast had called for calm seas. That was the first thing Danny Reyes remembered when I sat down with him three weeks after his rescue, his hands still bearing the peeling marks of prolonged saltwater exposure.

"You trust the forecast. You've done this a hundred times," Reyes said, staring at the coffee cup he hadn't touched. "And then the water just—it decides something different."

## The Trip

The *Marlene J*, a 34-foot commercial fishing vessel, departed the harbor at 4:47 a.m. on a Tuesday in early autumn, according to Coast Guard logs. Aboard were four men: Captain Robert "Bobby" Holloway, 58, a veteran of three decades on the water; Reyes, 41; and two younger crew members, Marcus Webb, 29, and Tyler Okafor, 24, a marine biology graduate student who had joined the crew part-time to fund his studies.

"Tyler wasn't even supposed to be there that day," said Holloway, whom I interviewed by phone from his home, where he is still recovering. His voice cracked. "He swapped shifts with another guy. That's the part I can't get past."

## When the Sea Turned

By 11 a.m., roughly eighteen nautical miles offshore, conditions changed with brutal speed. A localized squall—unforecasted and intense—brought swells the survivors estimated at twelve to fifteen feet.

"We took a wave broadside," Reyes recalled. "Then another before we could recover. Bobby was screaming to grab the life jackets. The boat just went over. One second you're standing, the next the whole world is upside down and green and cold."

The *Marlene J* capsized at approximately 11:20 a.m. The men had no time to issue a formal mayday, though the vessel's emergency position-indicating radio beacon (EPIRB) automatically activated upon submersion—a detail that Coast Guard officials would later credit with saving their lives.

## The Search

**Petty Officer First Class Amanda Cruz**, a search-and-rescue coordinator with the Coast Guard sector that received the distress signal, walked me through the response.

"The EPIRB gave us a position, but it's not a guarantee," Cruz explained. "In heavy seas, drift is significant. People move miles from where their beacon first pings. We launched an MH-60 helicopter and diverted a cutter, but we're searching for heads in the water—sometimes that's all you can see, a head between the swells."

**Lieutenant Commander David Osei**, who supervised the operation, was candid about the odds.

"Water temperature that day was around sixty-two degrees. That sounds survivable, but hypothermia sets in faster than people think. We were racing a clock, and honestly, the clock was winning for most of that afternoon."

The four men, meanwhile, had managed to reach the overturned hull. Only three life jackets had been recovered in the chaos.

## The Longest Hours

What followed was, in the words of all three survivors, a slow test of endurance and will.

"We took turns," Webb told me, the youngest surviving crewman. "The guy without the jacket would hold onto the two guys who had them. We rotated. Bobby made us rotate. He kept us organized even when I think he was worse off than any of us."

Captain Holloway, the oldest aboard, suffered a gash to his leg during the capsizing that bled steadily into the water—a fact none of the men spoke of aloud at the time, though all of them understood what blood in open ocean could attract.

"Nobody said the word 'shark,'" Reyes said quietly. "You just don't. But everybody's thinking it. Every time something brushed your leg, you'd feel your whole body lock up."

As the hours passed, Tyler Okafor began to falter.

"He was the youngest and the smallest," Holloway said. "He got cold fastest. He started talking about his mother, then he started not making sense. We knew what that meant."

Hypothermia produces confusion and drowsiness—a lethal combination in open water. The men took turns shouting at Okafor, shaking him, forcing him to answer questions to keep him conscious.

"I told him he still owed me twenty bucks," Webb said, allowing himself a small smile. "Made him say he'd pay me back. Kept making him say it."

## Rescue at Dusk

At 6:52 p.m.—more than seven hours after the capsizing—the crew of the Coast Guard helicopter spotted the overturned hull and four figures clinging to it.

"You never forget that sight," said **rescue swimmer Petty Officer Second Class Jenna Whitmore**, who was lowered into the water to reach the men. "Four people, and you can immediately see one of them is in serious trouble. You triage in your head on the way down."

Whitmore reached Okafor first.

"He was barely responsive. The others were adamant—'take him first, take him first.' In that kind of cold, after that many hours, these guys had every reason to think about themselves. They didn't. That's the thing I keep telling people."

All four men were hoisted to safety and transported to a regional medical center. Okafor was admitted in critical condition with severe hypothermia; the other three were treated for exposure, dehydration, and, in Holloway's case, the leg laceration that required forty stitches.

## The Aftermath

Tyler Okafor spent nine days in the hospital, four of them in intensive care. He survived.

**Coastal State University**, where Okafor is enrolled in the graduate marine biology program, issued a statement following his rescue:

> "Our entire university community is profoundly relieved that Tyler Okafor is recovering. # Five Survive Harrowing 26-Hour Ordeal in Open Water After Sailboat Sinks

**Coast Guard hails 'miraculous' rescue as survivors recount fight for their lives**

---

Five people are recovering today after being pulled from the open ocean following an extraordinary 26-hour battle for survival, their sailboat lost to the depths in a sudden overnight storm. Rescue officials are calling the operation one of the most challenging and remarkable recoveries in recent memory.

The group—two couples and a longtime friend, all experienced recreational sailors—had set out early Saturday morning for what was meant to be a weekend coastal cruise. By nightfall, worsening weather and a catastrophic hull breach turned their outing into a fight against exhaustion, hypothermia, and the vast, unforgiving sea.

## Disaster Strikes in the Dark

According to survivor accounts, the trouble began around 11 p.m. Saturday, when winds intensified far beyond the forecast and swells rose to more than 12 feet.

"We heard a crack, and then water was everywhere," said survivor Marcus Reyes, 42, speaking from a hospital bed where he is being treated for dehydration and exposure. "Within minutes, the boat was going down. We barely had time to grab the life raft and radio a mayday before she slipped under."

The vessel, a 34-foot sailboat, sank so rapidly that the crew was unable to deploy additional emergency supplies. With only a partially inflated life raft and their life jackets, the five clung together in the churning water as the storm raged around them.

Their distress signal, transmitted moments before the boat vanished, gave rescuers a starting point—but only a rough one. As hours passed, currents carried the survivors miles from their last known position.

## A Test of Endurance

Through the long night and the scorching day that followed, the group fought to stay alive and stay together. They tied themselves to one another and to the damaged raft with a length of rope, taking turns keeping watch and encouraging the weakest among them.

"There were moments I didn't think we'd make it," said Elena Vargas, 38, who suffered a leg injury during the sinking. "But we kept talking to each other. We kept each other awake. Every time someone wanted to give up, the others wouldn't let them."

Survivors reported battling relentless waves, the disorienting glare of the midday sun, and the creeping numbness of hypothermia despite the summer season. Dehydration set in quickly, and by the second day, several members of the group were drifting in and out of consciousness.

## The Search Intensifies

The Coast Guard launched a full-scale search-and-rescue operation shortly after receiving the mayday, deploying aircraft, cutters, and coordinating with nearby commercial vessels. But rough seas and low visibility hampered the effort throughout the night and into Sunday morning.

"Conditions were about as difficult as they get," said Petty Officer Daniel Cho, a spokesperson for the Coast Guard. "We were searching an expanding area of open water, with survivors who had no working beacon and were being pushed by the current. Time was absolutely critical."

Rescue crews flew grid patterns for hours, scanning the endless expanse of gray water for any sign of life. As the 24-hour mark passed, hope grew increasingly fragile.

## Spotted at Last

The break came just after 1 a.m. Sunday—roughly 26 hours after the sailboat went down. A Coast Guard aircrew, flying a final pass before refueling, caught a faint flicker in the darkness: one of the survivors had managed to activate a small waterproof flashlight, waving it desperately toward the sky.

"That tiny light was the difference between life and death," Officer Cho said. "If we'd been thirty seconds earlier or later, or looking in another direction, we might have missed them entirely."

A rescue swimmer was lowered into the heaving seas, reaching the exhausted group one by one. In a delicate operation lasting nearly an hour, all five were hoisted to safety, weak but alive.

"When I saw that swimmer come down out of the sky, I just started crying," Reyes recalled. "I couldn't believe it was real. These men and women risked everything to come find us out there. They're the reason we're alive."

## Recovering, and Grateful

All five survivors were transported to a regional medical center, where they are being treated for dehydration, exposure, and minor injuries. Doctors say all are expected to make a full recovery.

The Coast Guard credited the survivors' teamwork, discipline, and refusal to give up as key factors in their survival—alongside the persistence of the rescue crews who refused to call off the search.

"This is why we do what we do," said Officer Cho. "Twenty-six hours in open water is beyond what most people could endure. That they held on—and that our crews found them—it's nothing short of miraculous."

As she rested in her hospital room, Vargas offered a simple message for the crews who saved her life.

"Thank you," she said quietly. "There aren't words big enough. You gave us back our lives."
